title: Worst-case subset sum

problem.name: Subset sum
problem.statement_latex:
Given integers $a_1,\ldots,a_n,t$ in binary, find $x\in\{0,1\}^n$ with $\sum_i a_ix_i=t$, or decide that none exists. This entry concerns arbitrary inputs; the random density-one regime has separate, faster heuristic algorithms.
Quantum time is measured with coherent random-access memory and polynomial integer-arithmetic costs; classical bounds specify word-RAM operations and coefficient bit length.

quantum.details_latex: The $2n/7$ bound is a 2026 preprint result obtained from a worst-case seven-list sum algorithm, using quantum walks and coherent data structures. The $n/3$ construction uses a smaller precomputed sum list and quantum search over the remaining variables. Both bounds suppress polynomial arithmetic factors and require exponential accessible memory.

classical.headline_latex: $O(2^{0.49n})$ word operations for polynomial-bit inputs, OpenAI's worst-case subset-sum algorithm.
classical.details_latex: For each fixed $c$, the bound holds on all inputs of bit length $b\le n^c$ for sufficiently large $n$, with success probability at least $2/3$ and a running-time cap on every random execution. The word size is $O(n+b+\log n)$. A lower-space alternative uses $O^*(2^{n/2})$ time and $O^*(2^{0.199n})$ writable words, in particular $O(2^{n/5})$ words under a fixed polynomial-bit convention. For nonnegative inputs and small target $t$, pseudopolynomial algorithms with near-linear dependence on $n+t$ can be faster.

strength.description_latex: Polynomial speedup from $2^{0.49n}$ to $2^{2n/7}$. The fastest quantum result uses quantum walks; the $2^{n/3}$ algorithm uses amplitude amplification.

evidence.description_latex: Worst-case upper bounds with partial evidence for a speedup over classical algorithms. The strongest displayed quantum and classical bounds are 2026 preprints with their stated memory and bit-length assumptions.

hardware.description_latex: Polynomial active registers hold subset indices and integer sums; exponentially large coherent list and search structures dominate storage. Long walk or amplification sequences require fault tolerance. The classical low-space tradeoff provides a separate memory-sensitive comparison.

algorithm_items.content_latex: \href{https://arxiv.org/pdf/2608.07309}{Chukhin, Kulikov, Levitskii and Mihajlin, \emph{Improved Quantum Algorithms for Subset Sum and $k$-SUM} (2026)}.
